data.title: New 575kW Jetour Traveller 7 revealed: Rugged PHEV packs 245km EV range as Chinese brand prepares for Australia
data.description:
Australia-bound Jetour has revealed more details of its new Traveller 7, including a potent plug-in hybrid powertrain pumping out 575kW and 835Nm and offering up to 245km of claimed electric range.

Reservations for the new five-seat adventure SUV opened at the Chengdu motor show, where the Chery-owned brand revealed both petrol and PHEV versions.

The Traveller 7 is a larger addition to Jetour’s increasingly extensive family of squared-off adventure SUVs and follows the same basic design philosophy as the Traveller – known as the T2 in some export markets.

READ MORE: Shark hunter: Chery Stockman is the new name for the super-efficient plug-in hybrid diesel ute designed to overtake the BYD Shark 6 and Ford Ranger PHEV
READ MORE: 2026 Beijing Auto Show Greatest Hits: All the PHEVs, EVs, supercars and mega SUVs that will change the automotive game this year

That makes it particularly relevant to Australia, where Jetour is now actively establishing its local operation ahead of a planned launch in the first quarter of 2027.

The Traveller 7 has not been confirmed for Australia, but the T1 and T2 plug-in hybrids are already scheduled to lead the local rollout and the larger G700 off-roader will follow around six months later.

The headline version of the Traveller 7 is the C-DM PHEV, which combines a 1.5-litre turbo-petrol engine with three electric motors and all-wheel drive. Combined output is a hefty 575kW and 835Nm.

A large CATL battery provides up to 245km of electric-only driving under China’s CLTC testing regime, while Jetour claims a combined petrol-electric range of up to 1400km.

Those numbers make the Traveller 7 considerably more serious than the current Traveller C-DM, which offers up to 212km of claimed CLTC electric range from a 43.24kWh battery in its latest Chinese specification.

The Traveller 7 measures 4827mm long – stretching to 4848mm depending on specification – 2006mm wide and 1875mm high, with a 2800mm wheelbase.

Despite the 7 in its name, it remains a five-seater rather than adding a third row. Its larger body instead provides a roomier take on the Traveller formula, while the basic off-road recipe remains familiar: an upright body, high ground clearance, external spare wheel and side-hinged rear door.

The Traveller 7 C-DM also gets Jetour’s XWD intelligent all-wheel-drive system, selectable off-road driving modes and an automatic X mode that can adjust the drivetrain to suit the terrain.

Jetour quotes a 27-degree approach angle, 30-degree departure angle, 220mm minimum ground clearance and 700mm wading depth.

A petrol Traveller 7 is also available, using a 187kW/390Nm 2.0-litre turbo four-cylinder engine, eight-speed automatic transmission and XWD all-wheel drive.

Technology takes another step up in the PHEV, which is offered with Huawei’s Qiankun ADS 5 driver-assistance system, while the petrol model uses Jetour’s Falcon 500 system.

The cabin combines large digital displays with physical switches and can be equipped with 10-way electrically adjustable front seats, eight-point pneumatic massage, a reclining front passenger seat and 23-speaker audio.

The rear seats can also be arranged to help create a sleeping area around two metres long, underlining Jetour’s focus on camping and recreational use.

Full Chinese pricing has yet to be announced, with Jetour instead opening reservations at Chengdu with a 777-yuan deposit.

Jetour’s Australian operation is meanwhile taking shape, with local executives in place, dealer appointments underway and recruitment continuing ahead of the 2027 launch.

Jetour Australia’s own social media channels are now active, although the company is careful to state that specifications, features, availability and launch timing of overseas models remain subject to local confirmation.

There’s no confirmation yet that the Traveller 7 will be among them.

The post New 575kW Jetour Traveller 7 revealed: Rugged PHEV packs 245km EV range as Chinese brand prepares for Australia appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: JAC Hunter PHEV Cab Chassis confirmed: Australia’s cheapest plug-in ute gets work-focused BYD Shark 6 rival
data.description:
JAC will expand its new Hunter PHEV range with a cab-chassis version in early 2027, giving tradies and fleet operators a plug-in hybrid alternative to the BYD Shark 6 Dynamic Cab Chassis.

The new Hunter PHEV Cab Chassis has been confirmed for Australia following what JAC says has been strong demand from prospective fleet customers, more than half of whom have expressed interest in a cab-chassis version.

It will follow the Hunter PHEV dual-cab that has just gone on sale locally and is expected to retain the same petrol-electric drivetrain and core mechanical specification.

READ MORE: Electric SUVs on the agenda: Chinese giant JAC reveals Australian expansion plans
READ MORE: 2026 JAC Hunter X PHEV Review: Australia’s cheapest PHEV ute combines serious capability with useful EV range
READ MORE: Australia’s JAC Hunter PHEV tune goes global: Local engineering adopted for overseas markets

The announcement means the BYD Shark 6 will no longer have the Australian PHEV cab-chassis market to itself.

BYD launched its Shark 6 Dynamic Cab Chassis earlier this year priced from $55,900 plus on-road costs, making it the first PHEV cab-chassis ute offered locally.

JAC has not announced pricing for its cab-chassis, but there is potential for it to substantially undercut the BYD given the existing Hunter PHEV Pro dual-cab is priced from $49,988 plus on-road costs, while the better-equipped Hunter X costs $54,844 plus on-roads.

Final pricing, specifications and available configurations for the Cab Chassis will be announced closer to its early-2027 arrival. JAC says it will also announce genuine tray and body options before launch.

Rather than the factory tub fitted to the Hunter dual-cab, the Cab Chassis will provide an exposed rear platform allowing owners to install trays, canopies, toolboxes and other specialised bodies.

The Hunter Cab Chassis is expected to carry over the dual-cab’s plug-in hybrid drivetrain, which combines a 2.0-litre turbo-petrol engine with electric motors on the front and rear axles.

JAC claims maximum combined output of 360kW and quotes 1010Nm of driveline torque for the existing Hunter, although that torque figure is calculated by adding the outputs of the engine and electric motors rather than representing a directly measured system output.

A 31.2kWh lithium iron phosphate battery provides a claimed electric driving range of up to 100km, while the combination of the battery and 77-litre petrol tank produces a theoretical combined range of up to 1005km. Both range figures use the more generous NEDC testing standard.

JAC also quotes fuel consumption of 1.6L/100km under ADR81/02 testing, although, as with other PHEVs, the result depends heavily on starting the test with a charged battery and is not representative of fuel consumption once the battery’s usable charge has been depleted. The company itself notes the laboratory figure should be used for comparative purposes rather than as an indication of real-world consumption.

Importantly for commercial buyers, JAC expects the Cab Chassis to retain the Hunter’s 3500kg braked towing capacity. The competing $55,900 BYD Shark 6 Dynamic Cab Chassis is rated to tow 2500kg braked.

The JAC will also retain 3.3kW vehicle-to-load (V2L) capability, allowing its high-voltage battery to run compatible tools and other electrical equipment.

An Idle Charge function can use the petrol engine to replenish the battery while the vehicle is stationary, potentially allowing V2L equipment to continue operating at remote worksites where external electricity isn’t available.

JAC has yet to reveal the Cab Chassis’s payload, kerb weight or gross vehicle mass, figures that will be particularly important given its commercial focus.

The existing Hunter PHEV dual-cab has a payload of up to 915kg and a 3500kg braked towing capacity.

The Cab Chassis will also be covered by JAC’s seven-year/unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty, including commercial use, as well as seven years of capped-price servicing and roadside assistance. The high-voltage battery is covered for eight years or 150,000km.

The post JAC Hunter PHEV Cab Chassis confirmed: Australia’s cheapest plug-in ute gets work-focused BYD Shark 6 rival appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Revealed and confirmed! Kia PV7 electric van locked in for Australia with 460km-plus range, ultra-fast charging and up to nine seats
data.description:
Kia has confirmed its new PV7 electric van and people mover will come to Australia, with the PV5’s bigger brother locked in for a local launch in the final quarter of 2027.

Revealed in production form at the IAA Transportation show in Hannover, Germany, the PV7 is the second model in Kia’s dedicated Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) family and significantly ups the capability compared with the smaller PV5 already on sale in Australia.

Kia Australia has also confirmed the PV7 will undergo its local ride and handling development program ahead of launch, although pricing, model grades and final Australian specifications won’t be announced until closer to arrival.

READ MORE: Kia’s next electric van breaks cover! Bigger PV7 shapes up for Australia to battle Ford E-Transit, Farizon SuperVan, Renault Master E-Tech, LDV eDeliver9 and Mercedes-Benz eSprinter
READ MORE: Confirmed: Radical electric Kia PV5 people mover and cargo van coming to Australia. Ford Transit and Toyota HiAce fighter will make local debut this month
READ MORE: 2026 Kia PV5 Seven-Day Review: Who knew cargo vans only have two seats?

The headline numbers include a choice of 71.5kWh and 96.2kWh nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) batteries and an electric motor developing up to 200kW and 420Nm.

Front-wheel drive will be standard initially, but Kia has confirmed all-wheel-drive versions will be added later.

The Long Range Cargo fitted with the larger battery has a targeted WLTP driving range of more than 460km, although Kia says that figure is still subject to final homologation. Importantly for a working electric van, the PV7 steps up to an 800-volt electrical architecture.

Kia says that allows a 10-80 per cent recharge in the mid-20-minute range when connected to a 350kW DC fast charger.

In an unusual move, the PV7 can also be fitted with two charging ports: a front AC/DC connection and an optional AC port mounted towards the rear, potentially making it easier to plug in regardless of how the van is parked.

That represents a significant technical step beyond the smaller PV5 Cargo, which is already on sale in Australia from $55,990 plus on-road costs and uses a 71.2kWh battery, 120kW/250Nm front-mounted motor and 400V electrical architecture.

The seven-seat PV5 Passenger is also due in Australian showrooms in the final quarter of 2026.

At 5350mm long, 1995mm wide and 1990mm high on a 3500mm wheelbase, the PV7 is substantially larger than the 4695mm-long PV5 and moves Kia into a bigger commercial-vehicle class.

That means its logical Australian rivals include larger battery-electric vans such as the Ford E-Transit, Farizon SuperVan, Renault Master E-Tech, LDV eDeliver 9 and Mercedes-Benz eSprinter.

Kia will offer both Cargo and Passenger versions globally.

The PV7 Cargo Long provides up to 6.1 cubic metres of load volume, while the High Roof increases that to 8.0 cubic metres.

Maximum payload is rated at 1165kg for the Long and 1200kg for the Compact, while the Long has a low 550mm loading height and can swallow three Euro pallets.

Customers will eventually be able to choose between Compact, Long and High Roof Cargo bodies, Compact and Long Passenger versions and a dedicated Chassis Cab, along with various factory-backed conversions.

In all, Kia says it plans to develop 23 PV7 variants following the 2027 launch. An even larger PV9 is scheduled to follow in 2029.

The Passenger is potentially just as interesting for Australia. Globally, the PV7 Passenger will accommodate up to nine people, while Korean versions can seat as many as 11.

The seven-seat version gets Kia’s Long-Rail Easy Remove Seats, while nine-seat versions can be configured with or without a fourth seating row. Rear climate control and available 100W USB-C outlets are also included among the passenger-focused features.

Kia has not yet said which seating layouts will be offered in Australia.

As with the PV5, the PV7 is based on Kia’s dedicated E-GMP.S electric commercial-vehicle architecture rather than being converted from an existing combustion-engined van.

Its flat-floor layout is designed to make it easier for Kia to develop different bodies and conversions, while the PV7 also gets Vehicle-to-Load capability for powering tools and other electrical equipment.

There’s also a dedicated heavy-load driving mode that alters vehicle behaviour according to payload.

Inside, the PV7 gets 12.9-inch and 14.6-inch displays and Kia’s Android Automotive-based Pleos Connect operating system, including over-the-air updates, connected navigation and access to business-oriented applications.

The PV7 van has also been designed with frequent stops in mind, with an A-pillar grab handle, revised seating position and step geometry intended to make repeated entry and exit easier.

Safety equipment includes seven airbags -– including an unusual roof-mounted front passenger airbag -– along with autonomous emergency braking, lane keeping assistance, Highway Driving Assist 2.0, surround-view monitoring and remote parking functionality, although final Australian specifications are yet to be confirmed.

The PV7 will initially launch in Korea and Europe in the second half of 2027 before expanding into other markets. Pricing remains the major unknown.

The post Revealed and confirmed! Kia PV7 electric van locked in for Australia with 460km-plus range, ultra-fast charging and up to nine seats appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: MG’s new 845km EV costs how much? MG 07 sedan packs semi-solid battery tech and Tesla-fighting price
data.description:
MG has revealed full pricing and specifications for its new 07 electric sedan at the Chengdu motor show, including up to 845km of claimed range, semi-solid-state battery technology and bargain-basement Chinese pricing.

First revealed in May, the Tesla Model 3 and BYD Seal rival has now officially gone on sale in China with seven EV and plug-in hybrid variants priced from 108,900 to 159,900 yuan – roughly $23,000-$34,000.

The big news is what MG is offering for that money. Five versions are battery-electric, split between 67kWh semi-solid-state and larger 91kWh conventional lithium-ion batteries.

READ MORE: MG reveals large and sporty electric concept: The Cyber is shaping as a cut-price Ferrari Purosangue and BMW X5 rival
READ MORE: MG GO! concept revealed: Previews MG2 EV hatch to rival BYD Atto 1 and Geely EX2
READ MORE: Numbers up: MG chases S5 EV boost with more power and range but no price rise

The 67kWh battery, supplied by SAIC-backed Qingtao, powers versions with claimed CLTC ranges of 610km and 650km.

Those models use a 400V electrical architecture and a 176kW/300Nm front-mounted electric motor.

The flagship makes a substantial technical step up with a 91kWh CATL battery, 800V silicon-carbide electrical architecture and 5C fast-charging capability.

Its front electric motor produces 235kW and 350Nm and MG claims up to 845km of CLTC range and 0-100km/h acceleration in the five-second bracket.

That means the 07 isn’t simply one technical package with different battery capacities. The longest-range versions get substantially more sophisticated charging and electrical hardware than the cheaper semi-solid-state cars.

The semi-solid-state battery is arguably the most interesting development since MG first revealed the 07.

MG says the technology offers better resistance to puncture and extreme temperatures than conventional liquid-electrolyte cells while maintaining strong low-temperature charging performance.

The 07 is also offered as a plug-in hybrid, combining an 82kW 1.5-litre petrol engine with a 152kW electric motor and 30kWh CATL lithium iron phosphate battery.

MG claims 245km of electric-only range on the Chinese CLTC cycle and a huge 1745km total range with a fully charged battery and full tank. The PHEV battery can recharge from 30 to 80 per cent in a claimed 15 minutes.

The PHEV range opens at 108,900 yuan, while the 650km EV starts from 116,900 yuan – about $A25,000 on a straight currency conversion.

Even an 845km EV equipped with LiDAR is priced from 149,900 yuan, with the flagship topping out at 159,900 yuan.

There’s plenty of equipment, including mCDC adaptive dampers, MG’s VMC 2.0 vehicle-motion control system and, on selected versions, the Momenta R7 driver-assistance system and roof-mounted LiDAR first announced when the 07 was revealed.

Inside is a 15.6-inch 2.5K central touchscreen powered by a Qualcomm 8295P processor, while higher grades add features including a zero-gravity front passenger seat, electrically dimming panoramic roof and 21-speaker audio system.

Chinese buyers have responded strongly, with MG claiming 10,000 locked orders in less than two minutes after sales opened at Chengdu and more than 42,000 after 20 days.

There is still no confirmation the MG 07 will come to Australia to jojn the brand’s substantial EV and PHEV lineup.

The post MG’s new 845km EV costs how much? MG 07 sedan packs semi-solid battery tech and Tesla-fighting price appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Smart joins the EV price slashing frenzy! Also confirms #5 SUV is locked in for Australia
data.description:
Smart has slashed thousands of dollars from the prices of its #1 and #3 electric SUVs as it prepares to expand its Australian line-up with the larger Smart #5.

The Mercedes-Benz and Geely joint-venture brand which currently has only a niche presence in Australia through three east coast dealerships, has confirmed the all-electric #5 mid-size SUV is on its way here, although pricing and full launch details are being held back for a later announcement.

At the same time, Smart has slashed prices across the entire #1 and #3 ranges, cutting as much as $5000 from the price of its existing EVs.

READ MORE: Pint-sized Smart #2 caught testing: Paris motor show debut in October and Australia in 2027, but don’t expect a tiny price when it lands here
READ MORE: Aren’t Smarts meant to be small? Plug-in hybrid Smart #6 sedan sizes up BMW 5 Series and Benz E-Class
READ MORE: Get Smarter! Boxy 2025 Smart #5 Brabus squares up against the Tesla Model Y Performance and Hyundai Ioniq 5 N

The #1 Pro+ is now $49,900 plus on-road costs, down $5000 from its previous $54,900 price, while the Premium falls $5000 from $58,900 to $53,900. The high-performance Brabus has been reduced by $4000, from $67,900 to $63,900.

The #3 Pro+ is now $52,900 plus on-road costs, down $5000 from $57,900, while the Premium falls from $61,900 to $56,900 and the Brabus from $70,900 to $65,900.

That means five of the six Smart #1 and #3 variants have been cut by $5000, with only the #1 Brabus receiving a smaller $4000 reduction.

The reductions continue a broader trend of EV price repositioning in Australia as established brands face increasingly intense competition from a rapidly expanding field of Chinese electric cars.

The rear-wheel-drive #1 and #3 use a 200kW/343Nm electric motor and a 62kWh usable battery, while Brabus versions add a front motor to produce 313kW and 584Nm and all-wheel drive.

The bigger news for Smart’s longer-term Australian prospects is the arrival of the #5. Smart originally confirmed the mid-size electric SUV for Australia with expectations it would arrive during 2025, but that timetable came and went.

The company has now reconfirmed the #5 for Australia, describing its arrival as the next step in expanding its local range.

The Australian Smart website already lists Pro+ and Premium versions of the #5, both with claimed WLTP ranges of up to 590km, while also advertising the much more powerful #5 Brabus.

Significantly, the #5 represents a major technological step beyond the existing #1 and #3.

It employs an 800-volt electrical architecture that enables much faster DC charging, while overseas versions are available with a 100kWh battery.

The flagship #5 Brabus produces up to 475kW, can accelerate from 0-100km/h in 3.8 seconds and accepts DC charging at up to 400kW. Smart claims its 100kWh battery can be replenished from 10 to 80 per cent in 18 minutes and provides up to 540km of WLTP range.

Less extreme versions prioritise range, with Smart Australia quoting up to 590km for the Pro+ and Premium. Other features advertised locally include dual 13-inch OLED displays, a 230V vehicle-to-load power outlet and a cabin that can be converted into a camping-style bed.

Smart also points to the #5’s Euro NCAP Best-in-Class Large SUV award for 2025 and two Red Dot design awards.

Smart has previously confirmed development of a plug-in hybrid version of the SUV as the company backs away from its earlier EV-only strategy.

As EV Central has previously reported, the #5 PHEV employs technology sourced from Smart’s Geely parent and potentially gives the brand an alternative to mainstream electrified SUVs such as the Toyota RAV4, BYD Sealion 6 and Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV.

However, Smart’s latest Australian announcement is specifically focused on the all-electric #5. It makes no announcement about Australian availability of the PHEV and says its expanding local portfolio will comprise the #1, #3 and all-new #5 while continuing to offer all-electric mobility experiences.

The post Smart joins the EV price slashing frenzy! Also confirms #5 SUV is locked in for Australia appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program
data.description:
Hyundai is preparing a new generation of cheaper, faster-charging and longer-lasting batteries to underpin a massive global product offensive that will see more than 100 new or updated vehicles launched by the end of the decade.

The Korean auto giant has detailed an extensive battery development program that includes new in-house battery cells, a switch to significantly cheaper mid-nickel chemistry for upcoming EVs, smarter battery management and new technology designed to prevent thermal runaway spreading through a battery pack.

It comes as Hyundai prepares one of the largest product rollouts in its history, with more than 100 global launches and major model updates planned by 2030.

READ MORE: Revealed: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute tech will debut in Santa Fe SUV range extender
READ MORE: Hyundai Ioniq 3 priced: UK version of new EV rival for BYD and MG starts at $42,500 … that’s promising for Australia
READ MORE: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute delayed: It’s still coming to Australia but it could take until 2030 to get here

More than 18 will take Hyundai into new products or market segments and seven new vehicles are due within the next eight months alone.

The rollout will include conventional combustion-powered vehicles, hybrids, extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs) and battery-electric vehicles, with electrified models targeted to account for 60 per cent of Hyundai sales by 2030, up from 23 per cent in 2025.

Hyundai is targeting 5.55 million global vehicle sales and a six per cent global market share by the end of the decade.

Central to the technology push is Hyundai’s development of its own battery cells.

The company claims its new high-performance cells can produce more than twice the output of the high-nickel cells it has previously used while reducing charging time by 40 per cent.

The first application will be Hyundai’s new EREV powertrain arriving in the first half of 2027.

That system will initially appear in the new Santa Fe EREV, which Hyundai says will offer more than 600 miles – about 965km – of total driving range.

Hyundai says the EREV requires less than half the battery capacity of a comparable battery-electric vehicle while still providing equivalent battery performance and EV driving characteristics.

The technology is also significant for Australia because EREV is emerging as a leading candidate to power Hyundai’s upcoming body-on-frame midsize ute.

But Hyundai’s battery plans extend well beyond EREVs.

One of the biggest developments for conventional battery-electric vehicles will arrive from 2027.

Hyundai says EVs launching next year will adopt mid-nickel NCM – nickel-cobalt-manganese – battery cells that will reduce battery costs by around 30 per cent compared with the technology they replace.

Importantly, Hyundai claims the cheaper cells will maintain what it describes as “optimal performance” under real-world driving conditions.

The potential significance is substantial because the battery remains one of the most expensive individual components in an electric vehicle.

A 30 per cent reduction in battery cost does not mean the price of an entire Hyundai EV will fall by 30 per cent, but reducing the cost of the pack potentially gives the company much greater scope to lower vehicle prices – or fit larger batteries and more equipment without pushing prices higher.

It should also help Hyundai compete against the rapidly expanding number of lower-cost Chinese EV manufacturers.

The first models using the new mid-nickel batteries have not been identified.

However, they will arrive during an enormous expansion of Hyundai’s electrified range.

In Europe alone Hyundai plans to cover 85 per cent of the market with a fully electrified portfolio, including five new SUVs and light-commercial vehicles, while increasing annual EV sales from 116,000 in 2025 to more than 420,000 by 2030.

Hyundai isn’t concentrating purely on the chemistry inside the battery.

Software will increasingly be used to manage the battery throughout its working life.

Hyundai says an enhanced cloud-based battery management system (BMS) will extend the average life of its EV batteries by 20 per cent by 2028.

The system will monitor battery condition and use cloud connectivity to detect abnormalities in individual cells in real time.

That could have implications beyond how long owners can keep their cars.

Battery degradation and the cost of replacing an EV battery remain important considerations for used EV buyers, while improved battery longevity potentially increases residual values and extends the useful life of an electric vehicle.

Hyundai hasn’t detailed exactly how it has calculated its claimed 20 per cent average battery-life improvement or translated it into expected kilometres or years of service.

The other major component of Hyundai’s battery strategy is safety.

Hyundai has developed what it calls Thermal Runaway Protection (TRP), designed to prevent heat from a failing battery cell spreading into adjacent cells.

Thermal runaway occurs when a battery cell experiences an uncontrolled increase in temperature that can trigger further cells, potentially creating a chain reaction within the battery pack.

Rather than simply delaying the spread of heat, Hyundai claims its TRP system can block it at the source.

It combines a battery design that dissipates heat with barriers between individual cells intended to stop heat transfer.

Hyundai says the technology has been verified through more than 200 repeated tests using both prismatic and pouch-type NCM batteries.

The cloud-based BMS and TRP effectively provide two layers of defence.

The BMS is intended to detect abnormal behaviour early enough for preventative action to be taken, while TRP provides a physical defence against heat spreading if a cell does fail.

The new thermal-runaway technology will make its production debut with Genesis, with Hyundai’s roadmap identifying the upcoming electric GV90 flagship SUV as its first application.

The battery investment is part of a broader change in Hyundai’s electrification strategy.

Rather than relying exclusively on battery-electric vehicles, Hyundai is expanding across EVs, hybrids and EREVs as it pushes towards its 5.55-million annual sales target.

Among the models identified in the latest roadmap are the IONIQ 3, new-generation Tucson and Tucson Hybrid, Santa Fe EREV, a new electric SUV for India and new global and European B-segment SUVs.

Genesis will simultaneously expand beyond pure EVs with its first hybrid, the GV80 Hybrid, as well as an EREV SUV targeting more than 640 miles – around 1030km – of total range and the battery-electric GV90 flagship.

The post Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: What’s the deal with 800V? Why the EV tech that only matters some of the time should not be at the top of your shopping list
data.description:
Read a press kit for many new electric cars revealed recently and you could find a reference to 800 volts in it somewhere.

BMW’s new iX3 (pictured above). The Mercedes-Benz CLA. Porsche’s soon-to-arrive Cayenne Electric. Various cars from Zeekr, XPeng, Lotus and more.

Of course, the Porsche Taycan, Audi e-tron GT and various Kias and Hyundais have been using 800V architectures for years.

But recently the default is very much turning to the higher voltage.

Eight hundred volts is presented as a leap forward, and in one sense it is.

But it’s also arguably a tad over-hyped, at least for the vast majority of the time for most EV owners.

What 800V really means

An EV battery is a stack of individual cells wired together.

Each cell typically puts out somewhere around 3.6 volts for NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) batteries, or around 3.2V for LFP (lithium ferrous phosphate) batteries.

Wire them in series and the voltages add up; wire them in parallel and the capacity adds up.

They’ll still have the same amount of energy, but how they absorb and disperse it can be different.

Arrange them one way and you get a pack of around 400V, which is what most EVs have utilised until recently.

Arrange them another way and you can step the voltage up to 800 or more.

Even then, the voltage an EV puts out varies depending on how much charge is in the battery.

And the voltage is rarely 800V.

The Porsche Taycan is the car that started it all, yet even though it’s badged as an 800-volt system the original cars had a nominal voltage of 613V for the smaller battery and 723V for the larger battery.

And for that larger battery the voltage can swing from about 610 volts when flat to about 835 volts when full.

Voltage rises as state of charge rises, which is how the car monitors how much charge is left.

So an 800V system is not so much a hard and fast measurement, in the same way the 12V batteries used in all cars rarely put out 12 volts; they usually hover around  12.6 volts and get pushed to 14V or higher when the car is running.

When you see claims of how fast a car can charge it will often be relying on a high voltage – in the case of the upcoming Porsche Cayenne that’s 850V – and a lot of current (the amps required to get the power up).

Voltage ain’t power, but it helps achieve it

Anyone who remembers their high school physics will know that electrical power equals voltage multiplied by amps.

Ultimately, it’s the power that determines how fast the car will charge – but a higher voltage makes it easier to produce more power.

If you want to push 350kW into a battery at 400V, you need 875 amps. That’s a lot.

Push the same 350kW at 800V and you need less than 440 amps.

Compare that with the 10A maximum that a home powerpoint can put out and you can see we’re talking about big hits of electricity.

And those amps – the current – is the problem.

Current generates heat, and heat is the enemy of everything in the charging chain: including the cables and various connectors.

That’s why high-power charging cables can be liquid-cooled and very thick (and, therefore, heavy).

Double the current and you quadruple the resistive losses. Halve it and those losses drop off a cliff.

So doubling the voltage lets you move a lot more energy through the same hardware.

The main benefit with 800V is DC fast charging

An 800V architecture is almost entirely about public DC fast charging.

It affects almost nothing else with your ownership experience.

Charging at home on AC is identical no matter what the voltage of the battery pack.

Your home powerpoint – or EV charger – puts out about 230V, which is a whole heap less than what the battery is rated at.

It also goes through the car’s onboard charger to convert it from AC electricity coming out of the wall to DC electricity to be stored in the battery pack.

That onboard charger is typically 7kW, 11kW or 22kW, regardless of pack voltage.

An 800V Hyundai Ioniq 5 and a 400V Tesla Model Y plugged into the same wallbox overnight will do exactly the same thing at exactly the same rate.

For anyone charging predominantly at home – which is most EV owners, most of the time – 800V is a number on a brochure.

However, there are some secondary benefits.

Lower current means thinner cables and less copper inside the car, which saves a few kilograms and some cost.

For Porsche, the lower weight is important.

It’s a company that has built its reputation on performance, so every little bit counts.

Higher voltages also mean slightly lower losses under sustained high load.

That’s one reason electricity is transported at extremely high voltages (sometimes 500,000V) over big distances.

For Porsche and others chasing big performance, the higher voltage can help with repeatable track performance rather than just charging.

Really, though, the headline is faster charging.

Are there downsides to an 800V electrical system?

Higher voltage is harder and more expensive to engineer.

Every high-voltage component – inverters, DC-DC converters, compressors, contactors, insulation, connectors – has to be rated for the extra stress.

Silicon carbide semiconductors rated to 1200V are one solution, but they cost more than those used in a 400V EV.

Higher voltages also mean greater insulation to ensure safety.

And the big one: if the charger you’re using is limited to 400V then there’s zero benefit.

In some instances there could be negatives.

Roll up to the latest 300kW Tesla Supercharger, for example, and the limiting factor could be the current (amp) limit on the car.

The Hyundai Ioniq 5/6/9 are a good example.

Their DC charging typically tops out at about 320kW, which is 400A of current.

The cabling in the car, therefore, is limited to 400A, which at 400V is 160kW.

Similarly, the Porsche Macan is rated at up to 270kW of fast charging, but only on 800V. At 400V it’s limited to 135kW, again due to those current limits.

So even though the cars are capable of higher-powered charging, it relies on the 800V system to achieve that.

Can an 800V EV use a 400V charger?

All EVs can use all fast chargers, no matter what the voltage of the charger or what voltage the car is rated at.

That’s thanks to some simple but clever designs that allow the electrons to sort themselves out and everything to work as intended.

But there are different ways of achieving it.

The simplest way – and the way used by the Porsche Taycan, Audi e-tron and latest Mercedes-Benz CLA – is to use a DC-to-DC booster.

It steps the voltage up so that the battery sees 800V.

With its latest Macan, Porsche did without the need for that booster, instead essentially splitting the battery into two 400V banks and charging them concurrently when it sees a 400V load.

Hyundai and Kia used something quite clever, employing the motor as an inverter.

The rear inverter is reconfigured to act as a boost converter and the rear motor’s windings do the job of the inductor.

So there’s no additional hardware, no extra weight, although presumably there’s some tricky software to ensure it all works the way it should.

800V charging is limited, for now

Here’s where the enthusiasm needs tempering.

Australia’s ultra-rapid network – the 350kW and 450kW units from the likes of Evie, Chargefox, NRMA, Ampol and BP – will generally deliver above 800V and let an 800V EV maximise its charging speed.

But the far bigger slice of Australia’s public charging infrastructure is 400V, often limited to 50kW and 75kW hardware.

That includes the vast Tesla Supercharger network, much of it now open to all EVs.

That’s because all Teslas sold in Australia run a 400V system (the Cybertruck is the brand’s first 800V EV).

Tesla’s reasoning is that bigger, higher-draw vehicles benefit, smaller EVs with smaller batteries less so.

The other half of the answer is that Tesla built its way around the problem. Rather than raising voltage, it went hard on current: Model 3 and Model Y peak at 250kW on a 400V system.

Tesla owns its charging network, so it had the advantage of being able to optimise both ends of the equation.

Is it inevitable Tesla changes? Probably, but it’ll likely happen when a new platform demands it.

Why not go to 1000V or 2000V?

Higher voltage is generally better, right?

In many instances, yes, but it also creates challenges.

BYD’s Super e-Platform is a full 1000V architecture, paired with a battery capable of charging at up to 1000A, for a peak of 1000kW.

That’s the tech behind the “flash charging” sites Denza has committed to installing at Australian dealerships.

So, if 800 is better than 400, why isn’t everyone at 1500V or higher?

Essentially it comes down to safety.

We’ve all seen lightning, which is a high voltage burst of electricity travelling through thin air.

Air is an insulator, but only up to a point.

Push enough voltage across a gap and the air itself ionises and becomes conductive – you get an arc.

The higher the voltage, the wider the gap it can jump.

No amount of clever software gets around it.

Engineers solve the issue by providing more clearance – distance – between high voltage components where you don’t want a spark.

Go higher in voltage and components have to physically move further apart, in a car where nobody has spare room.

There’s also the issue of the plug.

The CCS2 Combo plug fitted to every EV now sold in Australia – including Teslas – tops out at 1000V.

Anything beyond means a new connector standard, which the EV world (rightly) is not in a rush to adopt.

Components dealing with higher voltages can also get expensive.

Besides, with circa-300km charging now down to 10 minutes or less – and BYD/Denza’s flash charging to halve that – it’s getting to the point where the gains are minimal.

Will all brands end up on 800V?

More and more cars are embracing 800V electrical systems, but not because 800V is magic.

It’ll happen because new platforms get designed once and live for a decade, because silicon carbide is getting cheaper every year, and because no car maker wants to be the one whose spec sheet says 400 when the rival’s says 800.

With bigger and more luxurious EVs it’s a no-brainer to head to 800V.

But we’d still expect cheaper city-focussed cars to stay 400V for a while yet, because an LFP hatchback with a 50kWh battery charging at 80kW has nothing to gain.

One point worth making is :don’t go buying an EV based on the voltage.

Buy it because of how it suits your needs and if the charging achieves what you need it to in terms of time taken.

A car that hits 350kW for 90 seconds and then falls off a cliff is not as good as one that sits at 180kW from 10 to 70 per cent.
